name: Sarawak-Malaysia My Second Home (S-MM2H)

requirements.blocker_text: Requires monthly income of at least RM 10,000, or alternatively liquid assets of at least RM 100,000, plus a RM 500,000 fixed deposit in a Sarawak-based bank (up to 50% withdrawable after 1 year for approved purposes including property, education, or medical expenses -- but not if the property was purchased more than 2 years before visa endorsement). No mandatory property purchase, unlike the Mainland programme.
requirements.fix_path: Document monthly income or liquid assets meeting the applicable threshold, and arrange the RM 500,000 fixed deposit.

requirements.blocker_text: The main applicant must be at least 30 years old -- notably younger than the Mainland MM2H programme's typical minimum, and with no age-tiered requirement structure.
Requires monthly income of at least RM 15,000, or alternatively liquid assets of at least RM 200,000, plus the same RM 500,000 fixed-deposit requirement as the single-applicant track.
requirements.fix_path: Document combined household income or liquid assets meeting the applicable threshold.

evidence_required.document: Income or liquid-assets documentation meeting the applicable single/family threshold
RM 500,000 fixed deposit placed in a Sarawak-based bank

outcome.physical_presence_requirement: minimum 15-30 days per year in Sarawak (sources vary on the exact figure), which can be split across multiple visits -- a materially lower bar than Mainland MM2H's commonly-cited 90-day figure

HONEST SOURCING GAP: no direct fetch of the Sarawak state government's own S-MM2H administering page was achieved in this research pass; sources checked disagree slightly on the exact minimum-stay figure (15 vs 30 days per year), flagged honestly in the physical_presence_requirement field rather than resolved by assumption. STRUCTURAL FINDING: S-MM2H is administered entirely independently by the Sarawak state government, not MOTAC (which runs the Mainland programme) -- a direct expression of Sarawak's autonomous immigration authority under the Malaysia Agreement 1963, and genuinely operated on different rules rather than being a regional variant of the same federal scheme. The most consequential real-world divergence, confirmed across multiple independent sources: when the federal government froze Mainland MM2H entirely in July 2020, Sarawak continued accepting S-MM2H applications throughout the freeze -- a concrete demonstration that Sarawak's programme functions as a genuinely separate legal instrument, not merely a rebranded regional office of the same scheme. A January 2025 revision to S-MM2H rules permits part-time work and business investment within Sarawak specifically -- the single biggest differentiator from Mainland MM2H's Silver/Gold tiers, which prohibit all work entirely; work_rights is modeled 'restricted' here to capture this real, if geographically confined, allowance. S-MM2H holders may reside anywhere in Malaysia except Sabah, per the visa's own terms -- a genuinely counterintuitive detail (the visa is named for Sarawak specifically, yet grants broader geographic reach than that), while Mainland MM2H holders' rights in Sarawak/Sabah are comparatively more restricted; this cross-jurisdictional patchwork is unique to Malaysia among every country documented in this dataset and is the clearest illustration anywhere in this build of how much a country's internal federal structure can shape its immigration-route landscape.
